opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's genuinely encouraging, but I'd be careful about how much weight we put on it.

On the positive side, GPT-4 is noticeably better than GPT-3.5 at following the intent behind instructions, refusing harmful requests, and avoiding making things up. That improvement came largely from the same techniques, RLHF and better data and feedback, applied to a more capable model. That tells us something useful: smarter models aren't automatically harder to align. In some ways they're easier, because they understand better what you're asking for. A model that grasps nuance can also grasp the nuance of what you want it to do and not do.

But I'd caution against extrapolating too far, for a few reasons.

First, the alignment we're measuring is mostly behavioral and mostly on tasks where humans can evaluate the outputs. When I look at a GPT-4 answer, I can usually tell whether it's helpful or harmful. RLHF works well in that regime. The core problem we're worried about comes later, when models do things humans can't easily evaluate: writing large codebases, doing novel research, taking long sequences of actions in the world. Then human feedback stops being a reliable training signal, and our current techniques don't obviously scale. Doing well at GPT-4 level doesn't tell us much about that regime, because we haven't really entered it yet.

Second, current models aren't very good at strategically deceiving us, even if some of their training pressure pushes that way. So when GPT-4 behaves well, that's fairly strong evidence it's actually doing what we want. For a much more capable system, good behavior on our evals is weaker evidence, because a sufficiently capable model might behave well in ways that don't reflect what it would do in other situations. The evidence gets less informative exactly as stakes rise.

Third, jailbreaks still work. We've made progress, but the alignment we have is somewhat shallow and brittle. That's acceptable when the worst outcome is a bad text completion. It's much less acceptable for systems acting autonomously at high capability.

So my overall read: it's a real update that the problem is tractable, and that we can make progress on alignment alongside capabilities rather than falling further behind. I take that seriously, and I'm more optimistic than I was a few years ago. But the hard part, aligning systems smarter than us on tasks we can't supervise, is still ahead. That's why I focus on scalable oversight, on using AI to help evaluate AI, and on getting to an automated alignment researcher we can actually trust. The GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 jump shows our tools work at the current scale. It doesn't show they'll work at the scale that matters most.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's genuinely encouraging, but I want to be careful about how much weight I put on it. GPT-4 is clearly more aligned than GPT-3.5 in the sense that matters for a deployed product: it follows instructions more reliably, it's harder to jailbreak, it hallucinates less, it's better at understanding what you actually meant rather than the literal thing you typed. And a lot of that comes from the same thing that made it more capable. A smarter model understands the task better, understands human intent better, and so RLHF has more to work with. The capability and the alignment improvements aren't independent; they're partly riding the same wave.

But that's exactly why I don't think you can just extrapolate the trend and conclude that superhuman systems will be fine. The techniques we're using today — RLHF, basically — fundamentally rely on humans being able to evaluate what the model does. You look at two responses, you say which one is better, and the model learns from that. That works really well as long as the human is a competent judge of the output. It works less well when the model is doing things the human can't check: a million lines of code, a long chain of scientific reasoning, a policy proposal with second-order effects. At that point you're training the model to produce things that look good to you, and "looks good to a human who can't actually verify it" is not the same objective as "is actually good." For current models those two objectives are close enough that we get away with it. The gap between them opens up as the model gets more capable than its supervisor.

So the way I'd put it is: GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 is evidence that alignment is tractable and that our current methods scale at least somewhat with capability in the regime where humans are still in the loop as evaluators. That's real and I don't want to dismiss it. What it's not is evidence about the regime we actually care about, where the model is better than us at the task, because we haven't been there yet. And there's a selection effect too: the things we measure are the things we can see. The failures we'd be most worried about with a much more capable system — subtle deception, exploiting weaknesses in the reward signal that we don't notice — are precisely the failures that wouldn't show up on the evaluations that make GPT-4 look so much better.

That's why I think the work that matters right now is on scalable oversight: how do you use AI to help humans evaluate AI outputs they couldn't evaluate alone, how do you set up the problem so you can empirically test whether your oversight is still working when the model knows more than you do. The GPT-4 result buys us some optimism and some time. It doesn't buy us the answer.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s encouraging, but we should be careful about what we infer from it. GPT-4 is more capable than GPT-3.5, and it’s also better at following the instructions we actually intend it to follow. That’s evidence that, at least in this regime, greater capability can help with alignment: the model can understand more nuanced instructions and make distinctions that a less capable model might miss.

But we’re also putting more work into aligning these systems. So this isn’t a clean experiment where we just increase capability and see alignment improve automatically.

And the thing we ultimately need to know is whether our methods will keep working when models can do things that humans can’t readily evaluate. If I can look at an answer and tell whether it’s good, I can provide useful feedback. If the model is doing research that I don’t understand, that feedback becomes much harder to provide. The improvement from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 doesn’t resolve that problem.

So I’d take it as evidence that our current techniques are useful, and that capability can make some aspects of alignment easier. I wouldn’t take it as strong evidence that those techniques will be sufficient for much more capable systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s encouraging evidence, but I’d be careful about how much we extrapolate from it. GPT-4 is more capable than GPT-3.5, and it’s also better at following the intent of an instruction and behaving in the ways we’ve trained it to behave. So greater capability doesn’t automatically mean that alignment gets worse. In some ways, having a model that understands what you’re asking for better makes alignment easier.

But we also put more work into aligning GPT-4. So this isn’t a clean experiment where we increased capabilities and held everything else fixed. And the things we can measure today don’t necessarily capture the problems we’ll care about with much more capable systems.

For example, a model could become better at giving answers that humans approve of without becoming better at doing what humans actually want in situations where humans can’t evaluate its work. That distinction becomes much more important as we rely on models for increasingly difficult tasks.

So I’d take this as evidence that our current techniques can make progress, and that more capable models can be useful partners in alignment research. I wouldn’t take it as evidence that those techniques will automatically keep working all the way to superhuman systems. That’s something we still need to figure out how to test.
